title: The Pronouns
summary: The personal pronouns, the two words for *we* that English cannot tell apart, the possessives that distinguish what is mine from what is ours, and the demonstratives that do duty for the third person — graded by respect, and running in a near series beside a far one.

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: Telugu has personal pronouns for the **first and second persons only**. There is no third-person pronoun proper: for *he*, *she* and *it* the language uses its demonstratives, which is why gender enters the third person and nowhere else (¶55).

paradigms.caption: The personal pronouns
paradigms.footnote: **మీరు** is the polite singular as well as the plural, exactly as *jūs* is in Lithuanian and *vous* in French. **నువ్వు** is used only to a close friend, a relative, an inferior or a child; the older books write it **నీవు**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.3–8.4.
sources.note: Source for the paradigm and for నువ్వు against మీరు.

rules.heading: The Two Words for *We*
rules.statement: **మేము** means *we* **excluding** the person spoken to; **మనం** means *we* **including** them. English *we* is ambiguous between the two; Telugu is not.

paradigms.caption: Inclusive and exclusive

rows.label: exclusive
cells: the speaker and others, but **not** the hearer
reporting to someone what your party did

rows.label: inclusive
cells: the speaker, the hearer, and any others
proposing, inviting, or speaking of the company you are both in

paradigms.footnote: Both take the same verb ending, -ము (¶71), so the pronoun is the only thing that carries the distinction and it cannot be dropped.

examples.gloss: We are here. You are there.
examples.note: the second sentence is what makes the exclusion audible
the possessive of మేము — and also the ordinary way to say *my* house (¶54)

footnotes: Krishnamurti and Gwynn’s illustration: if A says to B *we came home* meaning himself and others not including B, he says **మేము ఇంటికి వచ్చాము**; meaning himself and B, **మనం ఇంటికి వచ్చాము**.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.4(1).
sources.note: Source for the inclusive–exclusive distinction and the illustration.

rules.heading: The Possessive Stems
rules.statement: Each personal pronoun has a possessive stem used before a noun and invariable for gender, number and case: **నా, నీ, మా, మన, మీ**. As in ¶37, **నా** is only of what is the speaker's alone and **మా** of what is shared; **మన** is the possessive of మనం — *మన ఊరు*.

paradigms.caption: Nominative and possessive

rows.label: 1 sg.
cells: my — of what is mine alone

paradigms.footnote: The possessive stands **before** its noun and takes no ending of its own, so *నా పుస్తకం* and *నా పుస్తకాలు* are the same word twice — number is the noun’s business, not the possessive’s.

examples.note: a book is one’s own — నా
a household has other members — మా, though English says *my*

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §8.3, §8.4(4).
sources.note: Source for the possessive stems and for the నా / మా rule.

rules.heading: The Third Person, and How Much Respect It Carries
rules.statement: For the third person Telugu uses demonstratives, several for each gender, graded by respect. **వాడు** of a grown man is an insult, and **అది** of a woman is worse; the ordinary forms for a stranger are **అతను** or **ఆయన** of a man and **ఆమె** of a woman.

paradigms.caption: The third person of the distant series

rows.label: singular
cells: formal, and the ordinary polite choice

rows.label: singular
cells: very polite — a plural form used of one person

rows.label: plural
cells: one form for people of either sex (¶49)

paradigms.footnote: Of a thing there is only **అది** in the singular and **అవి** in the plural: things are not owed respect and have no grades.

examples.gloss: Who is he? (of a man one respects)

examples.note: అది of a thing carries no rudeness — only of a person

footnotes: వారు takes a plural verb even of one person, which is how respect is marked in the verb as well as in the pronoun.
A single person of the first degree of respect takes **వారు** and with it a plural verb, as Brown notes: *మా తండ్రి నాకు యిచ్చిరి*, "my father gave me", literally "our father gave (pl.)".

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §7.4–7.6.
sources.note: Source for the four degrees of respect and their labels.

sources.citation: Brown, Charles Philip, *A Grammar of the Telugu Language*, 2nd ed. Madras: Christian Knowledge Society's Press, 1857, p. 190.
sources.note: "A singular noun major (mahat) may often govern a plural verb."

rules.heading: The Near Series and the Far
rules.statement: Beside the **far** third-person series in **అ-** runs a **near** series in **ఇ-**, of what is close to the speaker: **ఇతను, ఈమె, ఇది, వీళ్ళు** against **అతను, ఆమె, అది, వాళ్ళు**. The two series are parallel — genders, respect, verb agreement — so ¶55 holds for both; this is the ఇ- / అ- opposition of ¶35.

paradigms.caption: The two series

rows.label: non-masculine sg.
cells: a woman, an animal, a thing

paradigms.footnote: Only the first letter differs between the columns. The far series is the commoner in speech, and is the unmarked choice where the situation calls for neither.

examples.target: ఇది నా పుస్తకం. అది మా ఇల్లు.
examples.roman: idi nā pustakaṁ. adi mā illu.
examples.gloss: This is my book. That is my house.
This one is my elder brother.

examples.note: near, masculine plural — persons of either sex

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §7.4.
sources.note: "Grammatically, the two series are exactly parallel, and hence whatever is said in the following paragraphs regarding the forms వాడు, అది, etc., applies equally to the forms వీడు, ఇది, etc."

vocabulary.gloss: he (very informal; rude of a stranger)
he (plural in form, the highest degree of respect, used of one person)

drills.stem: You are speaking to a friend and mean *we* — yourself and that friend. Which sentence is right?
drills.explanation: *మనం ఇక్కడ* includes the hearer. *మేము ఇక్కడ* would mean you and others, but not the person you are talking to.

drills.stem: **మీరు ఎవరు?** — said to one stranger. Why *మీరు* and not *నువ్వు*?
options: Because *మీరు* is the polite singular as well as the plural.
Because *నువ్వు* is only used of women.
drills.explanation: *మీరు* serves as both the plural and the polite singular, as *jūs* does in Lithuanian. *నువ్వు* is for a close friend, a relative, an inferior or a child.

drills.stem: You and your friends are here; the person you are talking to is somewhere else. Which sentence fits?
drills.explanation: *మేము* excludes the hearer; *మీరు అక్కడ* makes the exclusion plain. *మనం ఇక్కడ* would pull the hearer into the group.

drills.stem: **నేను రవి. నువ్వు మా అన్న.** What does **నువ్వు** mark about the relationship?
options: Familiar address — a close friend, a relative, a child.
drills.explanation: *నువ్వు* is the familiar singular, used to a close friend, a relative, an inferior or a child. To a stranger one would ask *మీరు ఎవరు?*

drills.stem: Which of these does Telugu **not** have?
options: A pronoun for *we* that excludes the hearer.
A pronoun for *we* that includes the hearer.
A third-person pronoun proper, distinct from the demonstratives.
A polite word for *you* in the singular.
drills.explanation: For *he*, *she* and *it* Telugu uses its demonstratives — the అ- and ఇ- series — and that is exactly why gender shows up in the third person and in no other. The other three it has: మేము, మనం and మీరు.

drills.stem: **___ ఇల్లు పెద్దది.** You mean the house you and your family live in. Which possessive?
drills.explanation: మా. A house is shared with the rest of the household, and నా is only for what belongs to the speaker alone — a book, a name. *మన ఇల్లు* would drag the person you are speaking to into the household as well, and *మీ ఇల్లు* would make it theirs.

drills.stem: Which of these are correct as they stand?
drills.explanation: *ఆమె నా అమ్మ* is the error: a mother is not one person’s alone, so మా. A book, a house shared with the hearer, and a name are all correctly possessed — the name being the clearest case of నా, since nobody else has it.

drills.stem: You are telling a friend where to meet. Which sentence puts the two of you in the same group?
drills.explanation: మనం includes the hearer, which is what an arrangement between two people needs. *మేము ఇక్కడ* tells the friend where your party is and leaves them out of it — the same English sentence, and the opposite social act.

drills.stem: **ఇతను** and **అతను** differ in their first letter only. What does the difference mark?
options: Nearness: ఇతను of someone close by, అతను of someone further off.
Gender: ఇతను is masculine and అతను non-masculine.
Number: ఇతను is singular and అతను plural.
drills.explanation: The ఇ- series is the near one and the అ- series the far, exactly as with ఇక్కడ and అక్కడ, ఇది and అది (¶35). Both are masculine, both singular, and both sit at the same degree of respect — the series and the respect grade are two independent choices.

drills.stem: Which of these pair a **near** word with the right description?
options: వీళ్ళు — these persons, of either sex
drills.explanation: ఇది is the *singular* — this woman, this animal, this thing — and its plural is ఇవి. The other three are right, and వీళ్ళు covers both sexes just as వాళ్ళు does (¶50): the near series reproduces the whole gender system and not merely the words.

drills.stem: Of **వాడు, అతను, ఆయన, వారు**, how many are of the **masculine** gender?
drills.explanation: All four. They differ in the respect they show and not at all in gender, which is why choosing among them is a social decision and never a grammatical one. Answering fewer usually means taking వారు for a plural — it is plural in *form*, and used of one man it is the politest word there is.

drills.stem: A learner says **అది మా అమ్మ** of their mother. The grammar is faultless. What is wrong?
options: అది is the impolite word for a woman; ఆమె or ఆవిడ is wanted.
అది is non-masculine and a mother is masculine.
drills.explanation: అది is the regular non-masculine singular and agrees perfectly — which is exactly the trap. Krishnamurti and Gwynn mark it *very informal, intimate, impolite* of a person. The gender is right, the possessive is right, and the sentence is still not one to say. Grammar and respect are different systems (¶55).

drills.stem: Match each third-person word with what it is used of. One entry in Column II is used by none of them.
columnII: a male person, spoken of with respect
a male person, spoken of without respect
a woman or a single thing
people of either sex, in the plural
animals or things, in the plural
drills.explanation: వాడు is the impolite word for a man and ఆయన the respectful one — the second option reverses them, which is the mistake that gives most offence. అది covers a woman and a thing alike in the singular (¶49), so the fourth option, which makes it plural, confuses number with gender. అవి is for things only; the third option gives it to people, forgetting that in the plural వాళ్ళు takes both sexes. "People of either sex, in the plural" belongs to వాళ్ళు, which is not in Column I.

drills.title: మనం ఎక్కడ?
drills.passage:
ఇది మా ఇల్లు. ఇతను మా అన్న. అతని పేరు రవి. ఈమె మా అమ్మ. వీళ్ళు మా స్నేహితులు. అవి నా పుస్తకాలు.
రవి: మనం ఇక్కడ. మీరు ఎక్కడ?
అమ్మ: మేము అక్కడ.
drills.romanization:
idi mā illu. itanu mā anna. atani pēru ravi. īme mā amma. vīḷḷu mā snēhitulu. avi nā pustakālu.
ravi: manaṁ ikkaḍa. mīru ekkaḍa?
amma: mēmu akkaḍa.
drills.translation:
This is my house. This is my elder brother. His name is Ravi. This is my mother. These are my friends. Those are my books.
RAVI: We are here. Where are you?
MOTHER: We are there.

questions.explanation: *ఇతను మా అన్న. అతని పేరు రవి.* The second sentence names nobody: అతని, *his*, carries the reference over from the first, which is what a pronoun is for.
*మేము అక్కడ*, says the mother. Note which word for *we* she chooses: మేము excludes Ravi, who has just asked where she is — had she said మనం she would have been claiming to stand where he stands.

questions.stem: Which statements about the passage’s pronouns are correct?
options: ఇతను and ఈమె are the near series; అతని refers back to ఇతను.
వీళ్ళు covers friends of either sex.
Ravi says మనం and his mother answers మేము, so the two are not in the same place.
అవి is used of the books because books are not persons.
questions.explanation: All four. The passage is built to put the whole system in nine lines: the near series against the far, one plural word for friends of both sexes (¶50), the inclusive against the exclusive *we*, and అవి for what is not a person (¶57).

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju & Gwynn, J. P. L., *A Grammar of Modern Telugu*. Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985, §7.4–7.6, §8.3–8.4.
sources.note: Source for the two series, the respect grades and the inclusive–exclusive pair the dialogue turns on.
